newsitem.title: CHINA: China considering signing human rights pacts.
newsitem.headline: China considering signing human rights pacts.

text.p: China said on Thursday it was considering signing two international human rights covenants, a move that would fulfil the first part of a U.S. plan to remove a key irritant in Sino-U.S. relations.
"We are actively considering these two covenants. We are actively studying and considering the question of joining," Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang said at a weekly news briefing.
"As to when we would join, however, that is entirely our own affair."

Tang's remarks were the first official indication that China may be moving towards an agreement with the United States on human rights, one of the chief strains on relations between Washington and Beijing.
U.S. officials had earlier played down expectations of a breakthrough, and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright ended her first visit to Beijing on Tuesday reporting no concrete progress.

On the eve of Albright's visit, The New York Times had said the two sides were close to a deal under which the United States would drop moves to censure China at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva in exchange for a series of Chinese concessions.

The commission's meeting in March and April is a traditional sparring ground for Washington and Beijing, and fresh clashes have been expected this year as U.S. officials vowed to press forward with a resolution slamming China's record.

The Times said that under the possible deal, China would sign the two international covenants, release a representative group of prisoners and resume talks with the International Committee of the Red Cross on visits to determine the status of prisoners of conscience in China.
Tang, while declining to discuss the covenants in detail, said diplomatic contacts on "avoiding tensions" at the Human Rights Commission had produced results.
"China hopes that this will help the cooperation of the two sides at the U.N. Human Rights Commission," he said.
Tang said Beijing had urged the United States to stop its moves to use the Geneva meeting as a platform to criticise Beijing, calling this "an erroneous policy".

The hint of a possible break in the Sino-U.S. standoff on human rights follows almost eight years of tension since China used tanks and troops to crush the 1989 Tiananmen Square pro-democracy protests.

The human rights issue, which Beijing has accused western powers of using in a cynical ploy to undercut China's rising regional power, has spilled over into trade links, with the United States repeatedly threatening sanctions.
Tang, however, marked the cordial new mood between Beijing and Washington, which both sides hope will culminate with an exchange of presidential visits over the next two years.

"At the moment, Sino-U.S. relations are showing signs of improvement and development. This is the result of the efforts of both China and the United States, and should be pursued by both sides," he said.
